1.15 Develop settings across editors

The metadata snapshots above compare two copies of the same files. A different question is how several editors set up the same photographs, for example after running Auto in Lightroom, Lightroom Classic and Capture One. develop_settings.py stores each editor’s settings as a separate, write-once capture in one archive:

Source (app) Reads Raw record kept
xmp Settings embedded in each DNG’s XMP, or in exported JPEGs with --extensions jpg (or dng,jpg), via ExifTool; or an existing compare_dng.metadata JSONL snapshot (--snapshot) All ExifTool tags
lrcat A Lightroom Classic catalog, opened read-only with the standard SQLite driver Settings text, digest, virtual-copy name, history step names
capture-one Capture One .cos settings files (default FOLDER/CaptureOne/Settings*) Complete XML 
uv run python develop_settings.py capture ARCHIVE lr xmp FOLDER
uv run python develop_settings.py capture ARCHIVE lrc lrcat FOLDER \
  --catalog CATALOG.lrcat
uv run python develop_settings.py capture ARCHIVE c1 capture-one FOLDER
uv run python develop_settings.py compare ARCHIVE lr lrc
uv run python develop_settings.py compare ARCHIVE lr c1 \
  --map XMP-crs:Exposure2012=CaptureOne:AL:Exposure

Each capture writes ARCHIVE/settings/LABEL.jsonl.gz (one record per photo: photo name, source identity, typed settings and the unchanged raw source) and LABEL.provenance.json (schema, source, photo count, record SHA-256, tool commit). A label is never overwritten. Typed settings use one namespace: Adobe settings as XMP-crs:<name>, whether they came from XMP or a catalog, and Capture One settings as CaptureOne:<block>:<name> (for example DL for the main adjustments and AL for the block holding automatic values). Text that is exactly a number or boolean is stored as one; everything else stays text.

settings.sqlite3 indexes every typed value; the setting_values view lists label, app, photo, tag, value_json, number. reindex rebuilds it from the captures after checking each record SHA-256. compare reports, per tag, the photos present in both captures, how many are identical (numbers by value), and for numbers the median and 90th-percentile differences and the correlation.

There are two implementations with the same command line and archive format:

Python develop_settings.py Rust develop-settings
Reads XMP with ExifTool (compare_dng.metadata) The XMP packet in a DNG’s first IFD or a JPEG’s APP1 segments, parsed directly
Records and provenance Pydantic models serde types
raw for xmp ExifTool tags and warnings The XMP packet text

Build the Rust one with make build-rust (or cargo build --release --bin develop-settings in rust-scanner) and run it as rust-scanner/target/release/develop-settings capture .... Both type values the same way, name settings by their XMP property (ExifTool’s ColorTemperature is recorded as XMP-crs:Temperature, its XMP name and Lightroom Classic’s), flatten structures to Parent/Field and write the same canonical value_json, so either can add captures to an archive, reindex it or compare it. test_develop_settings.py checks that both write equal records from the same fixtures and that each reindexes and compares the other’s captures identically.

1.15.1 Settings in rendered JPEGs

Exported JPEGs are a second place to find settings, and often the only record of what an export actually used:

Rendering Settings in the JPEG
Lightroom and Lightroom Classic exports The complete Camera Raw settings (crs:), including the Auto marker when Auto was applied
Capture One exports None; read the RAW folder’s .cos files instead
Out-of-camera JPEGs Only EXIF basics such as white balance mode, contrast, saturation and sharpness 
uv run python develop_settings.py capture ARCHIVE lr-export xmp EXPORT_FOLDER \
  --extensions jpg

A capture records which extensions it read in its provenance. The Rust reader takes the XMP from the JPEG’s APP1 segments, including Adobe’s extended XMP, whose chunks it assembles by GUID and offset. Exports are a good cross-check: in one 446-photo test, the settings embedded in Lightroom’s Auto exports matched the settings Lightroom had written into the DNGs on every photo, and the Lightroom Classic exports matched its catalog.

Capture One’s .cos files hold the current state, including any manual adjustment made after Auto; compare their modification times with the export times before treating them as the settings of an older export.

Limits:

  • An xmp capture reads the files and fails if one changes during the read. The Rust reader reads the XMP packet stored in a DNG’s first IFD or a JPEG’s APP1 segments.
  • Values are typed exactly: the Rust build parses floats with serde_json’s float_roundtrip, so every stored number reads back bit for bit.
  • Lightroom Classic computes Auto lazily and stores -999999 placeholders until a photo is rendered. lrcat refuses such photos unless --allow-pending is given, and then records the placeholders with a note.
  • Editors use different controls and scales. --map pairs tags; it does not claim that the controls are equivalent.
  • Captures describe settings; they do not reproduce rendered appearance and nothing is written back to photos, catalogs or settings files.
